blocks.body:
What should $(1/2)!$ mean? The factorial is defined by repeated multiplication, which only makes sense for whole numbers, yet formulas in probability, geometry and number theory keep producing $n!$ in places where $n$ wants to be a fraction or even a complex number. The gamma function is the standard answer: one function, given by an integral, that matches the factorial at the integers (shifted by one), obeys the same recursion everywhere, and extends to the whole complex plane apart from isolated poles.

In number theory the motivation is sharper. The Riemann zeta function satisfies a symmetric functional equation only after it is multiplied by a gamma factor, and the same holds for every $L$-function. The recursion, the poles, the reflection formula and the size of $\Gamma$ on vertical lines are therefore groundwork for the analytic theory of primes. Euler found the function in 1729, in letters to Christian Goldbach, while looking for a way to interpolate $n!$ between the integers.

blocks.title: An integral that produces factorials
blocks.body:
Start with a calculation. For an integer $n \ge 0$ put $I_n = \int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx$. Clearly $I_0 = 1$. Integrating by parts with $u = x^n$ and $dv = e^{-x}\,dx$ gives $I_n = \bigl[-x^n e^{-x}\bigr]_0^\infty + n\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}e^{-x}\,dx = n I_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$, because the boundary term vanishes at both ends. Hence $I_n = n!$.

Nothing in the integral forces $n$ to be an integer. For complex $s$ and $x > 0$ define $x^{s-1} = e^{(s-1)\log x}$; then $|x^{s-1}| = x^{\sigma-1}$ where $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$. At the end $x = \infty$ the factor $e^{-x}$ beats every power of $x$, so that half of the [[improper-integrals|improper integral]] always converges. Near $x = 0$ we have $e^{-x} \approx 1$, so convergence there is the same as convergence of $\int_0^1 x^{\sigma-1}\,dx$, which happens exactly when $\sigma > 0$.

blocks.title: The gamma function
blocks.body:
For complex $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$,
$$\Gamma(s) = \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx.$$
The integral converges absolutely in this half-plane, and it converges uniformly on every strip $a \le \operatorname{Re} s \le b$ with $0 < a < b$, so $\Gamma$ is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. By the calculation above, $\Gamma(n+1) = n!$ for every integer $n \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Functional equation of Γ
blocks.body:
For $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$,
$$\Gamma(s+1) = s\,\Gamma(s), \qquad \Gamma(1) = 1,$$
and consequently $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

Integrate by parts on $[\varepsilon, R]$:
$$\int_\varepsilon^R x^{s}e^{-x}\,dx = \bigl[-x^s e^{-x}\bigr]_\varepsilon^R + s\int_\varepsilon^R x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx.$$
As $\varepsilon \to 0^+$ the term $\varepsilon^s e^{-\varepsilon}$ tends to $0$, because $|\varepsilon^s| = \varepsilon^{\operatorname{Re} s}$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. As $R \to \infty$ the term $R^s e^{-R}$ tends to $0$. Taking both limits gives $\Gamma(s+1) = s\,\Gamma(s)$. Also $\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = 1$, and induction gives $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)\Gamma(n-1) = \dots = (n-1)!\,\Gamma(1) = (n-1)!$.

blocks.title: Continuing to the left
blocks.body:
The integral only defines $\Gamma$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, but the functional equation shows how to go further. Read backwards it says $\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(s+1)/s$. The right side makes sense for $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$, $s \ne 0$, and agrees with $\Gamma$ where both are defined. Repeating this $n$ times,
$$\Gamma(s) = \frac{\Gamma(s+n)}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n-1)},$$
which defines a meromorphic function on $\operatorname{Re} s > -n$ whose only possible poles are at $0, -1, \dots, -(n-1)$. Different choices of $n$ agree where they overlap, so by the uniqueness of [[continuation|analytic continuation]] there is exactly one meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ that equals the integral when $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. We keep calling it $\Gamma$.

A second construction makes the poles explicit and uses only [[series|power series]]. Split the integral at $x = 1$ and expand $e^{-x} = \sum_k (-1)^k x^k/k!$ on $[0,1]$; integrating term by term is allowed for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ because the series of absolute values converges. The result is
$$\Gamma(s) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^k}{k!\,(s+k)} + \int_1^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx.$$
The integral on the right converges for every complex $s$ and is an entire function of $s$. On any compact set avoiding $0, -1, -2, \dots$ the $k$-th term of the series is at most a constant times $1/k!$, so the series converges uniformly there and defines a meromorphic function. The right side is therefore the continuation of $\Gamma$, valid on all of $\mathbb C$.

blocks.title: Poles and residues
blocks.body:
$\Gamma$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$. Its only poles are simple poles at $s = 0, -1, -2, \dots$, and
$$\operatorname{Res}_{s=-k}\Gamma(s) = \frac{(-1)^k}{k!} \qquad (k = 0, 1, 2, \dots).$$

Use the series formula. Near $s = -k$ every term except the $k$-th is holomorphic, and so is the integral; the $k$-th term is $\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}\cdot\frac{1}{s+k}$. At points other than $0, -1, -2, \dots$ everything is holomorphic.

blocks.title: The value at 1/2 and the Beta integral
blocks.body:
Substituting $x = u^2$ in the definition gives $\Gamma(1/2) = \int_0^\infty x^{-1/2}e^{-x}\,dx = 2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du = \sqrt\pi$, the Gaussian integral. The functional equation then gives $\Gamma(3/2) = \tfrac12\sqrt\pi$ and $\Gamma(5/2) = \tfrac34\sqrt\pi$, and going left, $\Gamma(-1/2) = \Gamma(1/2)/(-1/2) = -2\sqrt\pi$. So the answer to the opening question is $(1/2)! = \Gamma(3/2) = \sqrt\pi/2$.

Products of gamma values come from a double integral. For $\operatorname{Re} a > 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} b > 0$ the Beta integral is $B(a,b) = \int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt$.

blocks.title: Euler's Beta integral
blocks.body:
For $\operatorname{Re} a > 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} b > 0$,
$$B(a,b) = \int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt = \frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.$$

Write $\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = \int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty x^{a-1}y^{b-1}e^{-(x+y)}\,dx\,dy$. The double integral converges absolutely, so we may change variables and use Fubini's theorem. Put $x = ut$, $y = u(1-t)$ with $u > 0$ and $0 < t < 1$. This maps the strip $(0,\infty)\times(0,1)$ bijectively onto the open quadrant, with Jacobian determinant of absolute value $u$. Since $x^{a-1}y^{b-1} = u^{a+b-2}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}$ and $x + y = u$,
$$\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = \int_0^\infty u^{a+b-1}e^{-u}\,du\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt = \Gamma(a+b)\,B(a,b).$$

blocks.title: Reflection formula
blocks.body:
For every $s \in \mathbb C \setminus \mathbb Z$,
$$\Gamma(s)\,\Gamma(1-s) = \frac{\pi}{\sin \pi s}.$$
In particular $\Gamma$ has no zeros, and $1/\Gamma$ is an entire function whose zeros are exactly $0, -1, -2, \dots$.

First let $0 < s < 1$. The Beta integral with $a = s$, $b = 1-s$ gives $\Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s) = \Gamma(1)B(s, 1-s) = \int_0^1 t^{s-1}(1-t)^{-s}\,dt$. The substitution $t = u/(1+u)$, which maps $(0,\infty)$ onto $(0,1)$ with $dt = du/(1+u)^2$, turns this into
$$\int_0^\infty \frac{u^{s-1}}{1+u}\,du.$$
This integral equals $\pi/\sin\pi s$. That is a standard [[residues|residue]] calculation, which we only sketch: integrate $z^{s-1}/(1+z)$ around a keyhole contour that hugs the positive real axis, with $\arg z \in (0, 2\pi)$. The small and large circles contribute nothing in the limit because $0 < s < 1$, the two sides of the cut contribute $(1 - e^{2\pi i s})$ times the integral, and the residue at $z = -1$ is $e^{i\pi(s-1)} = -e^{i\pi s}$. So the integral is $-2\pi i\,e^{i\pi s}/(1 - e^{2\pi i s}) = \pi/\sin \pi s$.

Both sides of the reflection formula are meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ and they agree on the interval $(0,1)$, so by the identity theorem they agree everywhere. Since $\pi/\sin\pi s$ never vanishes, $\Gamma(s)$ never vanishes. Finally $1/\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(1-s)\sin(\pi s)/\pi$: the poles of $\Gamma(1-s)$ at $s = 1, 2, \dots$ are cancelled by zeros of $\sin \pi s$, so $1/\Gamma$ is entire, and it vanishes exactly where $\Gamma$ has poles.

blocks.title: How big is Γ?
blocks.body:
For real $x \to \infty$, Stirling's formula says
$$\Gamma(x) \sim \sqrt{2\pi}\,x^{x-1/2}e^{-x},$$
which for $x = n+1$ is the familiar approximation of $n!$. More generally $\log\Gamma(s) = (s - \tfrac12)\log s - s + \tfrac12\log 2\pi + O(1/|s|)$ uniformly in any sector $|\arg s| \le \pi - \delta$. We omit the proof; it is in the references.

The consequence used most in number theory concerns vertical lines. For fixed real $\sigma$ and $|t| \to \infty$,
$$|\Gamma(\sigma + it)| \sim \sqrt{2\pi}\,|t|^{\sigma-1/2}e^{-\pi|t|/2}.$$
So $\Gamma$ decays exponentially as one moves up a vertical line. This is what makes contour integrals involving $\Gamma$ converge so well in the [[mellin|Mellin transform]], and it is how the gamma factor in the functional equation of $\zeta$ controls the size of $\zeta$ to the left of the critical strip.

blocks.title: Gaussian moments and negative half-integers
blocks.body: Evaluate $\int_0^\infty x^4 e^{-x^2}\,dx$ and $\Gamma(-3/2)$.
blocks.solution:
Substitute $x = \sqrt u$, so $dx = \tfrac12 u^{-1/2}\,du$. The integral becomes
$$\tfrac12\int_0^\infty u^{3/2}e^{-u}\,du = \tfrac12\Gamma(5/2) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac12\sqrt\pi = \frac{3\sqrt\pi}{8}.$$
The same substitution shows $\int_0^\infty x^m e^{-x^2}\,dx = \tfrac12\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac{m+1}{2}\bigr)$ for every real $m > -1$.

For $\Gamma(-3/2)$ run the recursion backwards: $\Gamma(-1/2) = \Gamma(1/2)/(-1/2) = -2\sqrt\pi$, and $\Gamma(-3/2) = \Gamma(-1/2)/(-3/2) = \tfrac43\sqrt\pi$. In general $\Gamma$ is positive on $(0,\infty)$, negative on $(-1,0)$, positive on $(-2,-1)$, and so on: the sign changes at each pole.

blocks.title: Trigonometric integrals from the Beta function
blocks.body: Compute $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^6\theta\,d\theta$.
blocks.solution:
In the Beta integral substitute $t = \sin^2\theta$, so $1 - t = \cos^2\theta$ and $dt = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$. This gives the general identity
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2a-1}\theta\,\cos^{2b-1}\theta\,d\theta = \tfrac12 B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{2\,\Gamma(a+b)}.$$
For $\sin^6\theta$ take $2a - 1 = 6$ and $2b - 1 = 0$, that is $a = 7/2$, $b = 1/2$. Since $\Gamma(7/2) = \tfrac52\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac12\sqrt\pi = \tfrac{15}{8}\sqrt\pi$ and $\Gamma(4) = 6$,
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^6\theta\,d\theta = \frac{\tfrac{15}{8}\sqrt\pi\cdot\sqrt\pi}{2\cdot 6} = \frac{15\pi}{96} = \frac{5\pi}{32}.$$

blocks.title: Γ on vertical lines
blocks.body: Show that for real $t$, $|\Gamma(\tfrac12 + it)|^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{\cosh\pi t}$, and for real $t \ne 0$, $|\Gamma(it)|^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{t\sinh\pi t}$.
blocks.solution:
First, $\overline{\Gamma(s)} = \Gamma(\bar s)$. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ this follows by conjugating the integrand, and it extends to all $s$ through the formula $\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(s+n)/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n-1))$, whose right side has the same property.

So $|\Gamma(\tfrac12+it)|^2 = \Gamma(\tfrac12+it)\Gamma(\tfrac12-it)$. The reflection formula with $s = \tfrac12 + it$, so that $1 - s = \tfrac12 - it$, gives
$$\frac{\pi}{\sin(\tfrac\pi2 + i\pi t)} = \frac{\pi}{\cos(i\pi t)} = \frac{\pi}{\cosh \pi t}.$$
For the second formula, $|\Gamma(it)|^2 = \Gamma(it)\Gamma(-it)$, and the functional equation gives $\Gamma(1 - it) = -it\,\Gamma(-it)$. Hence
$$\Gamma(it)\Gamma(-it) = \frac{\Gamma(it)\Gamma(1-it)}{-it} = \frac{\pi}{-it\,\sin(i\pi t)} = \frac{\pi}{-it\cdot i\sinh\pi t} = \frac{\pi}{t\sinh \pi t}.$$
Both formulas show the decay $|\Gamma(\sigma+it)| \approx \sqrt{2\pi}\,|t|^{\sigma-1/2}e^{-\pi|t|/2}$ predicted by Stirling: for instance $\pi/\cosh \pi t \approx 2\pi e^{-\pi|t|}$.

blocks.title: Gauss's limit and Wallis's product
blocks.body:
Prove Gauss's formula $\Gamma(s) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{n!\,n^s}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)}$ for real $s > 0$, and deduce Wallis's product
$$\frac{\pi}{2} = \prod_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(2k)^2}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $g_n(s) = \int_0^n x^{s-1}(1 - x/n)^n\,dx$. Substituting $x = nu$ and using the Beta integral,
$$g_n(s) = n^s\int_0^1 u^{s-1}(1-u)^n\,du = n^s B(s, n+1) = \frac{n^s\,\Gamma(s)\,n!}{\Gamma(s+n+1)}.$$
By the functional equation $\Gamma(s+n+1) = (s+n)(s+n-1)\cdots s\,\Gamma(s)$, so $g_n(s) = \dfrac{n!\,n^s}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)}$.

On the other hand, for $0 \le x \le n$ we have $0 \le (1 - x/n)^n \le e^{-x}$, because $\log(1 - y) \le -y$, and $(1 - x/n)^n \to e^{-x}$ for each fixed $x$. By dominated convergence, with dominating function $x^{s-1}e^{-x}$, we get $g_n(s) \to \Gamma(s)$.

Now take $s = \tfrac12$. Then $s(s+1)\cdots(s+n) = \dfrac{1\cdot 3\cdots(2n+1)}{2^{n+1}}$, so
$$\frac{2^{n+1}\,n!\,\sqrt n}{1\cdot3\cdots(2n+1)} \to \sqrt\pi.$$
Square this and write $(2^n n!)^2 = \prod_{k=1}^n(2k)^2$ and $\bigl(1\cdot3\cdots(2n+1)\bigr)^2 = (2n+1)\prod_{k=1}^n(2k-1)(2k+1)$. The squared quantity becomes
$$\frac{4n}{2n+1}\prod_{k=1}^n\frac{(2k)^2}{(2k-1)(2k+1)} \to \pi.$$
Since $4n/(2n+1) \to 2$, the partial products of Wallis's product tend to $\pi/2$.

blocks.body:
- $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$, not $n!$. The shift by one is a historical convention (the letter $\Gamma$ and the shift are due to Legendre); $\Gamma(n+1) = n!$ is the safe form to remember.
- The integral formula is valid only for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. For $\operatorname{Re} s \le 0$ the integral diverges, and $\Gamma(s)$ means the continuation, computed for example by $\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(s+n)/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n-1))$.
- Matching the factorial at the integers does not single out $\Gamma$: for any constant $c$, the function $\Gamma(s)(1 + c\sin 2\pi s)$ has the same integer values and the same recursion. On $(0,\infty)$ the Bohr–Mollerup theorem characterises $\Gamma$ as the only function $f$ with $f(1) = 1$, $f(x+1) = x f(x)$ and $\log f$ convex.
- $\Gamma$ never vanishes. The negative integers are poles of $\Gamma$ and zeros of $1/\Gamma$.
- Stirling's formula is an asymptotic statement about the ratio: $\Gamma(x)/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,x^{x-1/2}e^{-x}) \to 1$, while the difference grows without bound.

The [[mellin|Mellin transform]] is built on the integral that defines $\Gamma$: $\Gamma(s)$ is the Mellin transform of $e^{-x}$, and Mellin inversion gives $e^{-y} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\Gamma(s)\,y^{-s}\,ds$ for $c > 0$, the starting point for smoothed sums over integers.

For the [[zeta|Riemann zeta function]], the substitution $x = \pi n^2 t$ in $\Gamma(s/2)$ turns $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)n^{-s}$ into $\int_0^\infty e^{-\pi n^2 t}t^{s/2-1}\,dt$. Summing over $n$ connects $\zeta$ with the theta function of [[fourier-poisson|Poisson summation]], and the result is the symmetric [[functional-equation]] for $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$. The trivial zeros of $\zeta$ at $-2, -4, \dots$ are the poles of $\Gamma(s/2)$ seen from the other side.

Outside number theory, $\Gamma$ gives the volume $\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac n2 + 1)$ of the unit ball in $\mathbb R^n$, and the normalising constants of the gamma, chi-squared and Student distributions in [[distributions|probability]].

1. Show that $\Gamma(n + \tfrac12) = \dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n\,n!}\sqrt\pi$ for every integer $n \ge 0$.
2. Show that $B(a,b) = \displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{u^{a-1}}{(1+u)^{a+b}}\,du$ for $a, b > 0$.
3. Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1(-\log x)^{s-1}\,dx = \Gamma(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
4. Check that the residues $(-1)^k/k!$ of $\Gamma$ at $s = -k$ are consistent with the reflection formula, by computing the residue of $\pi/(\sin(\pi s)\,\Gamma(1-s))$ at $s = -k$.

blocks.body:
Suppose you want the sum of $f(n)$ over all integers $n$, and $f$ is spread out, so the sum converges slowly. Poisson summation replaces it by the sum of the Fourier transform $\hat f$ over the integers, and a spread-out function has a concentrated transform. The two sides can look completely different, and the identity between them is one of the most useful tools in analysis and number theory.

Its most famous application is Riemann's. Applied to a Gaussian, Poisson summation gives the transformation law $\theta(1/t) = \sqrt t\,\theta(t)$ for the theta function $\theta(t) = \sum_n e^{-\pi n^2 t}$, and from that law Riemann derived the functional equation of the zeta function.

blocks.title: Fourier series in brief
blocks.body:
A function $g:\mathbb R \to \mathbb C$ with period 1 can often be written as a superposition of the waves $e^{2\pi i kx}$, $k \in \mathbb Z$ (see [[complex-numbers]] and [[trig]] for $e^{i\phi} = \cos\phi + i\sin\phi$). The key fact is orthogonality:
$$\int_0^1 e^{2\pi i jx}\,\overline{e^{2\pi i kx}}\,dx = \int_0^1 e^{2\pi i (j-k)x}\,dx = \begin{cases} 1 & j = k,\\ 0 & j \ne k.\end{cases}$$
So if $g(x) = \sum_k c_k e^{2\pi i kx}$ with $\sum_k|c_k| < \infty$, multiplying by $e^{-2\pi i kx}$ and integrating term by term recovers the $k$-th Fourier coefficient
$$c_k = \hat g(k) = \int_0^1 g(x)\,e^{-2\pi i kx}\,dx.$$
The converse question, whether $g$ really equals its Fourier series, needs hypotheses. We use one standard fact without proof: a continuous 1-periodic function whose Fourier coefficients satisfy $\sum_k|\hat g(k)| < \infty$ equals the sum of its Fourier series at every point. (It is equivalent to the statement that a continuous periodic function with all Fourier coefficients zero is identically zero.)

Smoothness makes the coefficients small. If $g$ is periodic with a continuous second derivative, integrating by parts twice gives $\hat g(k) = -\widehat{g''}(k)/(4\pi^2k^2)$ for $k \ne 0$, so $|\hat g(k)| \le C/k^2$ and the fact applies.

blocks.title: Fourier transform
blocks.body:
For an integrable function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$, the Fourier transform is
$$\hat f(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx \qquad (\xi \in \mathbb R).$$
It measures how much of the frequency $\xi$ is present in $f$. With $2\pi$ placed in the exponent, the formulas below carry no stray constants.

blocks.title: Rules of the transform, and the Gaussian
blocks.body:
Three rules follow by substituting in the [[riemann-integral|integral]]:
- translation: $f(x - a)$ has transform $e^{-2\pi i a\xi}\hat f(\xi)$;
- modulation: $e^{2\pi i bx}f(x)$ has transform $\hat f(\xi - b)$;
- dilation: for $\lambda > 0$, $f(\lambda x)$ has transform $\lambda^{-1}\hat f(\xi/\lambda)$.

The dilation rule is the uncertainty principle in miniature: squeezing $f$ by a factor $\lambda$ stretches $\hat f$ by the same factor.

The Gaussian $G(x) = e^{-\pi x^2}$ is its own transform. Let $F = \hat G$. Differentiating under the integral sign, which the rapid decay of $G$ allows, and using $G'(x) = -2\pi x\,G(x)$,
$$F'(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty(-2\pi i x)\,G(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx = i\int_{-\infty}^\infty G'(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx.$$
Integrating by parts (the boundary terms vanish) turns the last integral into $2\pi i\xi\,F(\xi)$, so $F'(\xi) = -2\pi\xi\,F(\xi)$. This is the differential equation that $G$ itself satisfies, so $F(\xi) = F(0)e^{-\pi\xi^2}$, and $F(0) = \int e^{-\pi x^2}\,dx = 1$. Combining with the dilation rule ($\lambda = \sqrt t$): for $t > 0$, the function $e^{-\pi t x^2}$ has transform $t^{-1/2}e^{-\pi\xi^2/t}$. A narrow Gaussian has a wide transform, and vice versa.

blocks.title: Poisson summation formula
blocks.body:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be continuous, and suppose there is a constant $C$ with $|f(x)| \le C(1+|x|)^{-2}$ and $|\hat f(\xi)| \le C(1+|\xi|)^{-2}$ for all real $x$ and $\xi$. Then for every real $x$
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} f(x+n) = \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\hat f(k)\,e^{2\pi i kx},$$
and in particular
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} f(n) = \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\hat f(k).$$
Both series converge absolutely.

Let $P(x) = \sum_n f(x+n)$, the periodisation of $f$. By the decay of $f$ the series converges absolutely and uniformly for $x \in [0,1]$, and $P$ has period 1, so $P$ is continuous and periodic. Its Fourier coefficients are
$$\hat P(k) = \int_0^1\sum_n f(x+n)\,e^{-2\pi i kx}\,dx = \sum_n\int_n^{n+1} f(y)\,e^{-2\pi i ky}\,dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)\,e^{-2\pi i ky}\,dy = \hat f(k).$$
Here we swapped sum and integral (uniform convergence), substituted $y = x + n$, and used $e^{-2\pi i k(y-n)} = e^{-2\pi i ky}$. By hypothesis $\sum_k|\hat f(k)| < \infty$, so by the fact quoted above $P$ equals its Fourier series: $P(x) = \sum_k\hat f(k)\,e^{2\pi i kx}$. Setting $x = 0$ gives the second formula.

blocks.title: What the proof says
blocks.body: The proof is worth remembering for its idea. Wrapping $f$ around a circle of length 1 produces a periodic function, and the Fourier coefficients of that periodic function are the values of $\hat f$ at the integers. Summing a function over the lattice $\mathbb Z$ and summing its transform over the same lattice are two descriptions of one object.

blocks.title: Transformation law of θ
blocks.body:
For $t > 0$ let $\theta(t) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} e^{-\pi n^2 t}$. Then
$$\theta(1/t) = \sqrt t\,\theta(t).$$

Apply Poisson summation to $f(x) = e^{-\pi t x^2}$. By the previous section $\hat f(\xi) = t^{-1/2}e^{-\pi\xi^2/t}$, and both $f$ and $\hat f$ decay faster than any power, so the theorem applies:
$$\theta(t) = \sum_n f(n) = \sum_k t^{-1/2}e^{-\pi k^2/t} = t^{-1/2}\,\theta(1/t).$$
Multiply by $\sqrt t$.

blocks.title: What the theta relation says
blocks.body:
As $t \to 0^+$ the terms $e^{-\pi n^2 t}$ decay slowly and $\theta(t)$ is a long sum of numbers close to 1. The transformation law evaluates it almost exactly:
$$\theta(t) = t^{-1/2}\,\theta(1/t) = t^{-1/2}\bigl(1 + 2e^{-\pi/t} + 2e^{-4\pi/t} + \cdots\bigr).$$
So $\theta(t)$ is $t^{-1/2}$ up to an error that is exponentially small in $1/t$. This is the general pattern: when $f$ is spread out, $\hat f$ is concentrated near $0$, and one side of Poisson summation is dominated by a single term.

Riemann's use of this relation, explained in [[functional-equation]], passes through the [[mellin|Mellin transform]]: $\int_0^\infty\tfrac12(\theta(t) - 1)\,t^{s/2-1}\,dt = \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$, and the symmetry $t \leftrightarrow 1/t$ of $\theta$ becomes the symmetry $s \leftrightarrow 1-s$ of the completed zeta function.

blocks.title: The finite version
blocks.body:
The same ideas work on the finite group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, where all sums are finite and convergence never arises. Write $e(x) = e^{2\pi i x}$. Orthogonality is now the geometric series identity
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} e\!\left(\frac{an}{N}\right) = \begin{cases} N & \text{if } N \mid a,\\ 0 & \text{if } N\nmid a,\end{cases}$$
and the discrete transform $\hat f(a) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(n)\,e(-an/N)$ satisfies the inversion formula $f(n) = \frac1N\sum_{a=0}^{N-1}\hat f(a)\,e(an/N)$. The first identity detects the congruence $a \equiv 0 \pmod N$ by an exponential sum; this is the starting point of the [[circle-method|circle method]] and of Fourier-analytic [[additive-combinatorics|additive combinatorics]].

blocks.title: A sum that is almost exactly 10
blocks.body: Show that $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z} e^{-\pi n^2/100}$ differs from $10$ by less than $10^{-100}$.
blocks.solution:
The sum is $\theta(1/100)$. By the transformation law with $t = 100$,
$$\theta(1/100) = \sqrt{100}\,\theta(100) = 10\Bigl(1 + 2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-100\pi n^2}\Bigr).$$
Since $n^2 \ge n$, the inner sum is at most $\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-100\pi n} = e^{-100\pi}/(1 - e^{-100\pi}) < 1.5\,e^{-100\pi}$. So the sum equals $10 + \varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 30\,e^{-100\pi}$. Finally $e^{-100\pi} = 10^{-100\pi/\ln 10} < 10^{-136}$, so $\varepsilon < 3\cdot10^{-135}$.

Summing directly, the terms $e^{-\pi n^2/100}$ only drop below $10^{-15}$ once $|n| \ge 34$, so dozens of terms are needed for ordinary floating-point accuracy, and the closeness to 10 is invisible from the series itself.

blocks.title: A partial-fraction identity and the Basel problem
blocks.body:
Let $a > 0$. Prove that
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\frac{1}{n^2 + a^2} = \frac{\pi}{a}\coth(\pi a),$$
and deduce that $\sum_{n\ge1} 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$.
blocks.solution:
Let $g(x) = e^{-2\pi a|x|}$. Its transform is
$$\hat g(\xi) = 2\int_0^\infty e^{-2\pi a x}\cos(2\pi x\xi)\,dx = \frac{2\cdot 2\pi a}{(2\pi a)^2 + (2\pi\xi)^2} = \frac{a}{\pi(a^2+\xi^2)},$$
using $\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha x}\cos(\beta x)\,dx = \alpha/(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$ for $\alpha > 0$. The function $g$ is continuous and decays exponentially, and $\hat g(\xi) \le C(1+|\xi|)^{-2}$, so Poisson summation applies:
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-2\pi a|n|} = \frac{a}{\pi}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\frac{1}{a^2+k^2}.$$
With $q = e^{-2\pi a}$, the left side is $1 + 2q/(1-q) = (1+q)/(1-q) = \coth(\pi a)$. Rearranging gives the identity.

For the Basel problem, separate the term $k = 0$:
$$2\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{1}{k^2+a^2} = \frac{\pi}{a}\coth(\pi a) - \frac{1}{a^2}.$$
Using $\coth y = \frac1y + \frac y3 + O(y^3)$ as $y \to 0$, the right side equals $\frac{\pi^2}{3} + O(a^2)$. On the left, each term increases to $1/k^2$ as $a \downarrow 0$, so by monotone convergence the left side tends to $2\sum_{k\ge1}1/k^2$. Hence $\sum_{k\ge1}1/k^2 = \pi^2/6$.

blocks.title: When the hypotheses fail
blocks.body: Test Poisson summation on the indicator function of $[0,1]$, that is $f(x) = 1$ for $0 \le x \le 1$ and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise. What goes wrong, and how is it repaired?
blocks.solution:
On the left, $\sum_n f(n) = f(0) + f(1) = 2$. On the right, $\hat f(0) = \int_0^1 dx = 1$ and, for $k \ne 0$, $\hat f(k) = \int_0^1 e^{-2\pi i kx}\,dx = 0$. So $\sum_k\hat f(k) = 1 \ne 2$.

The theorem does not apply: $f$ is discontinuous and $\hat f(\xi) = (1 - e^{-2\pi i\xi})/(2\pi i\xi)$ decays only like $1/|\xi|$. Look at the periodisation $P(x) = \sum_n f(x+n)$: it equals $1$ for every non-integer $x$ and $2$ at the integers. Fourier coefficients are integrals and cannot see the values at single points, so the Fourier series of $P$ is the constant 1.

The standard repair is to assign the average of the one-sided limits at each jump: with $f(0) = f(1) = \tfrac12$, the left side becomes $1$ and the formula holds. For functions with jumps, this averaging convention is part of the correct statement.

blocks.body:
- Conventions vary: books use $e^{-ix\xi}$, $e^{-2\pi i x\xi}$, with or without a factor $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$. Under another convention $e^{-\pi x^2}$ is no longer its own transform and Poisson summation acquires constants. Check the convention before quoting a formula.
- Poisson summation needs hypotheses: decay of both $f$ and $\hat f$, or a careful treatment of discontinuities as in the last example. Convergence of both sides alone does not guarantee that they are equal.
- The theta law is $\theta(1/t) = \sqrt t\,\theta(t)$, not $\theta(1/t) = \theta(t)/\sqrt t$. Test at an extreme value: for large $t$, $\theta(t)$ is close to 1, while $\theta(1/t)$ is large, about $\sqrt t$.
- A shift on one side becomes a phase on the other: $\sum_n f(x+n)$ corresponds to $\sum_k\hat f(k)e^{2\pi i kx}$, not to a shifted sum of $\hat f$.

- [[functional-equation]]: Riemann's proof of the functional equation of $\zeta$ is the theta law fed through a Mellin transform. Twisting the theta function by a Dirichlet character gives the functional equations of [[l-functions|Dirichlet L-functions]], with a [[gauss-sums|Gauss sum]] arising as the transform of the character.
- [[large-sieve]]: the large sieve inequality bounds a trigonometric polynomial $\sum a_n e(n\alpha)$ at well-spaced points $\alpha$; its proofs rest on the duality between a sequence and its transform.
- [[exponential-sums]] and [[circle-method]]: by orthogonality on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, the number of representations $N = n_1 + \dots + n_k$ is $\int_0^1 S(\alpha)^k e(-N\alpha)\,d\alpha$ for a suitable exponential sum $S$. Poisson summation also converts a long exponential sum into a shorter dual sum, a basic step in estimating such sums.
- [[additive-combinatorics]]: Roth's theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions and many sumset estimates are proved with Fourier analysis on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$.
- [[navier-stokes]]: Fourier introduced his trigonometric series in the Théorie analytique de la chaleur (1822) to solve the heat equation. In fluid mechanics the transform turns derivatives into multiplication by $2\pi i\xi$, which is how energy estimates and scaling arguments for the Navier–Stokes equations are organised.

1. Verify the translation, modulation and dilation rules from the definition of $\hat f$.
2. Apply Poisson summation to $f(x) = e^{-\pi t(x+a)^2}$ to show that $\sum_n e^{-\pi t(n+a)^2} = t^{-1/2}\sum_k e^{-\pi k^2/t}e^{2\pi i ka}$ for $t > 0$ and real $a$.
3. Compute $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}1/(n^2+1)$ to six decimal places in two ways: by direct summation and from the identity in the second example. Roughly how many terms does the direct sum need?
4. Show that $\theta(t) - t^{-1/2}$ tends to $0$ faster than any power of $t$ as $t \to 0^+$.

blocks.body:
A Dirichlet series $F(s) = \sum a_n n^{-s}$ packages arithmetic information into a function of a complex variable. The questions we care about, however, concern partial sums: how many primes there are up to $x$, or how large $\sum_{n\le x} d(n)$ is. The Mellin transform is the dictionary between functions of $x$ on $(0,\infty)$ and functions of $s$ in a vertical strip, and Perron's formula is its most important entry: it recovers $\sum_{n \le x} a_n$ from $F$ by integrating $F(s)x^s/s$ up a vertical line.

Once a partial sum is a contour integral, complex analysis takes over. The contour is moved to the left, and every pole of $F(s)x^s/s$ that is crossed leaves a term behind. This is the mechanism behind the prime number theorem and the explicit formula.

blocks.title: Mellin transform
blocks.body:
For a function $f$ on $(0,\infty)$, its Mellin transform is
$$\mathcal Mf(s) = \int_0^\infty f(x)\,x^{s-1}\,dx,$$
defined for those complex $s$ where the integral converges absolutely. Since $|x^{s-1}| = x^{\operatorname{Re}s - 1}$, this set is a vertical strip $\alpha < \operatorname{Re} s < \beta$ (possibly a half-plane, possibly including an edge line), whose edges are fixed by the behaviour of $f$ near $0$ and near $\infty$. A Mellin transform is always a function together with its strip.

blocks.title: First examples and rules
blocks.body:
Four basic examples:
- $f(x) = e^{-x}$: $\mathcal Mf(s) = \Gamma(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. This is the definition of [[gamma|the gamma function]].
- $f(x) = 1/(1+x)$: $\mathcal Mf(s) = \pi/\sin\pi s$ for $0 < \operatorname{Re} s < 1$ (Example 1).
- $f(x) = 1$ on $(0,1)$ and $0$ on $[1,\infty)$: $\mathcal Mf(s) = \int_0^1 x^{s-1}\,dx = 1/s$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
- $f(x) = 0$ on $(0,1]$ and $-1$ on $(1,\infty)$: $\mathcal Mf(s) = -\int_1^\infty x^{s-1}\,dx = 1/s$ for $\operatorname{Re} s < 0$.

The last two have the same formula $1/s$ in different strips. The strip is part of the data.

Two rules are used constantly. Scaling: for $a > 0$, $f(ax)$ has transform $a^{-s}\mathcal Mf(s)$. Summation: if $\sum_n|a_n|n^{-\sigma} < \infty$ and $\int_0^\infty|f(x)|x^{\sigma-1}\,dx < \infty$, then on the line $\operatorname{Re} s = \sigma$ the function $\sum_n a_n f(nx)$ has transform $F(s)\,\mathcal Mf(s)$, where $F(s) = \sum a_n n^{-s}$. For instance
$$\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\sum_{n\ge1}a_n e^{-nx}\Bigr)x^{s-1}\,dx = \Gamma(s)F(s).$$

Finally, the substitution $x = e^{-u}$ gives $\mathcal Mf(\sigma + it) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(e^{-u})e^{-\sigma u}e^{-itu}\,du$, a Fourier transform of $f(e^{-u})e^{-\sigma u}$ (in the convention without $2\pi$ in the exponent). Facts about the [[fourier-poisson|Fourier transform]] therefore carry over; in particular Fourier inversion becomes Mellin inversion.

blocks.title: Mellin inversion
blocks.body:
Suppose $\int_0^\infty|f(x)|x^{c-1}\,dx < \infty$, that $t \mapsto \mathcal Mf(c+it)$ is integrable on $\mathbb R$, and that $f$ is continuous at the point $x > 0$. Then
$$f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\mathcal Mf(s)\,x^{-s}\,ds.$$
This is Fourier inversion after the change of variables above; we do not reprove it.

blocks.title: Smoothed sums
blocks.body:
Applied to $e^{-x}$, inversion gives the Cahen–Mellin integral
$$e^{-y} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\Gamma(s)\,y^{-s}\,ds \qquad (y > 0,\ c > 0),$$
which converges absolutely because $|\Gamma(c+it)|$ decays like $e^{-\pi|t|/2}$. Now let $F(s) = \sum a_n n^{-s}$ converge absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > \sigma_a$, take $c > \max(0, \sigma_a)$, put $y = n/x$, multiply by $a_n$ and sum. Absolute convergence of everything allows the swap, and
$$\sum_{n\ge1}a_n e^{-n/x} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}F(s)\,\Gamma(s)\,x^s\,ds.$$
The left side is a smoothly weighted version of $\sum_{n\le x}a_n$: terms with $n$ much smaller than $x$ get weight close to 1, terms with $n$ much larger get weight close to 0. The exponential decay of $\Gamma$ makes the integral easy to handle. To recover the sharp partial sum we need a kernel that is exactly 1 for $n < x$ and exactly 0 for $n > x$. That kernel is $x^s/s$.

blocks.title: Perron's lemma
blocks.body:
Let $c > 0$ and $y > 0$, and for $T > 0$ put
$$I(y,T) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}\frac{y^s}{s}\,ds.$$
Then $I(y,T) \to \delta(y)$ as $T \to \infty$, where $\delta(y) = 1$ for $y > 1$, $\delta(1) = \tfrac12$, and $\delta(y) = 0$ for $0 < y < 1$. More precisely,
$$|I(y,T) - \delta(y)| \le \frac{y^c}{\pi T\,|\log y|}\quad (y \ne 1), \qquad |I(1,T) - \tfrac12| \le \frac{c}{\pi T}.$$

Let $y > 1$. For large $U > 0$ integrate $y^s/s$ counterclockwise around the rectangle with vertices $c - iT$, $c + iT$, $-U + iT$, $-U - iT$. The only pole inside is $s = 0$, with residue $y^0 = 1$, so the integral over the right edge equals $2\pi i$ minus the integrals over the other three edges. On the left edge $|y^s/s| \le y^{-U}/U$, so that edge contributes at most $\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot 2T\cdot y^{-U}/U$ to $I$, which tends to $0$ as $U \to \infty$. On each horizontal edge $|s| \ge T$, so each contributes at most
$$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{c}\frac{y^\sigma}{T}\,d\sigma = \frac{y^c}{2\pi T\log y}.$$
Hence $|I(y,T) - 1| \le y^c/(\pi T\log y)$.

If $0 < y < 1$, use the rectangle reaching right to $\operatorname{Re} s = U$ instead. There is no pole inside, the far edge contributes at most $\frac{T}{\pi}\,y^U/U \to 0$, and each horizontal edge at most $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_c^\infty\frac{y^\sigma}{T}\,d\sigma = \frac{y^c}{2\pi T|\log y|}$. So $|I(y,T)| \le y^c/(\pi T|\log y|)$.

If $y = 1$, compute directly with $s = c + it$, $ds = i\,dt$:
$$I(1,T) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{dt}{c+it} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{c\,dt}{c^2+t^2} = \frac{1}{\pi}\arctan\frac{T}{c},$$
since the odd part $-it/(c^2+t^2)$ integrates to zero. Then $\tfrac12 - I(1,T) = \frac1\pi\arctan\frac cT \le \frac{c}{\pi T}$.

blocks.title: Perron's formula
blocks.body:
Let $F(s) = \sum_{n\ge1}a_n n^{-s}$ converge absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > \sigma_a$, and let $c > \max(0, \sigma_a)$ and $x > 0$. Then
$${\sum_{n\le x}}' a_n = \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}F(s)\,\frac{x^s}{s}\,ds,$$
where the prime means that when $x$ is an integer the last term $a_x$ is counted with weight $\tfrac12$. Quantitatively, for every $T > 0$,
$$\Bigl|{\sum_{n\le x}}' a_n - \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}F(s)\,\frac{x^s}{s}\,ds\Bigr| \le \sum_{n\ne x}\frac{|a_n|\,(x/n)^c}{\pi T\,|\log(x/n)|} + \frac{c\,|a_x|}{\pi T},$$
the last term being present only when $x$ is an integer.

On the segment from $c - iT$ to $c + iT$ the series for $F$ converges absolutely and uniformly, so we may integrate term by term:
$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}F(s)\,\frac{x^s}{s}\,ds = \sum_n a_n\,I(x/n, T).$$
By Perron's lemma, $I(x/n,T)$ differs from $\delta(x/n)$ by at most the stated amounts, and $\delta(x/n)$ is $1$ for $n < x$, $\tfrac12$ for $n = x$ and $0$ for $n > x$, so $\sum_n a_n\delta(x/n) = \sum'_{n\le x}a_n$. This proves the inequality.

The right side tends to $0$ as $T \to \infty$. For $n \ge 2x$ we have $|\log(x/n)| \ge \log 2$, so those terms contribute at most $\frac{x^c}{\pi T\log 2}\sum_n|a_n|n^{-c}$, a finite constant divided by $T$. The finitely many terms with $n < 2x$ each carry a factor $1/T$. Letting $T \to \infty$ gives the limit formula.

blocks.title: Moving the contour
blocks.body:
Perron's formula is useful because the integrand $F(s)x^s/s$ can often be continued to the left of the line $\operatorname{Re} s = c$. If $F$ continues meromorphically and has controlled growth, one replaces the segment $[c - iT, c + iT]$ by $[c' - iT, c' + iT]$ with $c' < c$. By the [[residues|residue theorem]] the difference is $2\pi i$ times the residues in between, plus two horizontal integrals. Each residue becomes a term of an asymptotic formula, and the integral along the new line, where $|x^s| = x^{c'}$ is smaller, becomes part of the error term.

The model case is $F = \zeta$ with $a_n = 1$, where the sum is $\lfloor x\rfloor$. The pole of $\zeta$ at $s = 1$ contributes the residue $x$, the main term. The pole of $1/s$ at $s = 0$ contributes $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$, which is the average value of $\lfloor x\rfloor - x = -\{x\}$; the oscillation of $\{x\}$ stays in the remaining integral.

For $F = -\zeta'/\zeta = \sum\Lambda(n)n^{-s}$ (see [[chebyshev]]) the sum is $\psi(x)$. The pole at $s = 1$ gives the main term $x$, and each zero $\rho$ of $\zeta$ is a pole of $-\zeta'/\zeta$ and contributes $-x^\rho/\rho$. Pushing the contour all the way to the left is the [[explicit-formula]]; showing that the zeros contribute $o(x)$, which needs a [[zero-free-region]] to the left of $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, proves the [[pnt|prime number theorem]].

blocks.title: A 2026 claim
blocks.body:
This concept is linked to the [[quasi-rh|quasi-Riemann hypothesis]] for a specific reason. On 30 September 2026 a manuscript attributed to an OpenAI internal model claimed that every Dirichlet $L$-function is zero-free in the half-plane $\operatorname{Re} s > \tfrac78$. According to the claim, the argument uses Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, cubic theta sums and a Mellin continuation, and the proof is reported to have been verified in Lean. This is a claim, not an established theorem, and we say nothing about its details beyond this.

What "Mellin continuation" means in general is the technique of this lesson. One writes a function as a Mellin integral that converges in some strip, splits the integral at $x = 1$, and uses a transformation law of the integrand to show that each piece continues beyond the strip. The classical example is Riemann's proof of the [[functional-equation]] of $\zeta$, where the transformation law is $\theta(1/t) = \sqrt t\,\theta(t)$.

blocks.title: The Mellin transform of 1/(1+x)
blocks.body: Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{s-1}}{1+x}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{\sin\pi s}$ for $0 < \operatorname{Re} s < 1$, and relate the edges of the strip to the poles of the right side.
blocks.solution:
Near $x = 0$ the integrand has size $x^{\sigma-1}$ ($\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$), which is integrable exactly when $\sigma > 0$; near $\infty$ it has size $x^{\sigma-2}$, integrable exactly when $\sigma < 1$. So the strip is $0 < \sigma < 1$.

For real $s \in (0,1)$ substitute $x = t/(1-t)$, so $dx = dt/(1-t)^2$, $1 + x = 1/(1-t)$ and $x^{s-1} = t^{s-1}(1-t)^{1-s}$. The integrand becomes $t^{s-1}(1-t)^{-s}$, so the integral is $B(s, 1-s) = \Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s)$, which equals $\pi/\sin\pi s$ by the reflection formula of [[gamma]]. Both sides are holomorphic in the strip and agree on $(0,1)$, so they agree throughout the strip.

The right side has poles at $s = 0$ (residue $1$) and $s = 1$ (residue $-1$), exactly on the edges. They record the behaviour of $f$: $1/(1+x) \approx 1$ near $0$, and $\int_0^1 x^{s-1}\,dx = 1/s$; while $1/(1+x) \approx 1/x$ near $\infty$, and $\int_1^\infty x^{s-2}\,dx = -1/(s-1)$. In general, a term $x^{-a}$ in the expansion of $f$ at $0$ produces a pole at $s = a$ with the same coefficient.

blocks.title: Asymptotics from poles
blocks.body:
Use the Mellin transform to explain the expansion
$$\frac{1}{e^y - 1} = \frac1y - \frac12 + \frac{y}{12} + O(y^{5/2}) \qquad (y \to 0^+)$$
in terms of values of the zeta function.

blocks.title: Perron's lemma in numbers
blocks.body: Take $c = 1$ and $T = 50$. Compute $I(y,T)$ numerically for $y = 2$, $y = \tfrac12$ and $y = 1$, and compare with the error bounds in Perron's lemma.
blocks.solution:
With $s = 1 + it$ the imaginary parts cancel by symmetry, and
$$I(y,T) = \frac{y}{\pi}\int_0^T\frac{\cos(t\log y) + t\sin(t\log y)}{1+t^2}\,dt.$$
Numerical integration gives:
- $y = 2$: $I \approx 1.01828$, so the error is about $0.01828$, while the bound $2/(50\pi\log 2)$ is about $0.01837$.
- $y = \tfrac12$: $I \approx -0.00458$, while the bound $\tfrac12/(50\pi\log 2)$ is about $0.00459$.
- $y = 1$: $I = \frac1\pi\arctan 50 \approx 0.49363$, an error of about $0.00637$, against the bound $1/(50\pi) \approx 0.00637$.

The bounds are nearly sharp here, and the convergence is slow: the error decays only like $1/T$. This is why practical applications choose $T$ as a function of $x$ and estimate the truncation error together with the shifted integral, and why smoothed sums, with their exponentially decaying kernels, are preferred whenever the problem allows them.

blocks.body:
- Perron's integral converges only conditionally: $|x^s/s|$ decays like $1/|t|$, which is not integrable. The integral means $\lim_{T\to\infty}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}$, and in practice one works with the truncated version and its error term. The compact form $\sum_{n\le x}a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}F(s)\frac{x^s}{s}\,ds$ is shorthand that hides this limit, the conditions $c > 0$ and $c > \sigma_a$, and the halving of the term $n = x$ when $x$ is an integer.
- The line of integration must lie to the right of both $0$ and the abscissa of absolute convergence. On another line one is inverting a different Mellin transform (compare the two functions with transform $1/s$ above).
- The truncation error is large for $n$ close to $x$, because $|\log(x/n)|$ is small. Bounding that part requires information about the $a_n$ near $x$, and it is often the delicate step.
- Moving a contour needs bounds for $F$ on the horizontal segments, not just a meromorphic continuation.

- [[functional-equation]]: Riemann's proof writes $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ as the Mellin transform of $\tfrac12(\theta(t) - 1)$ at $s/2$, and continues it by splitting at $t = 1$.
- [[pnt]]: Perron's formula for $-\zeta'/\zeta$ together with a zero-free region gives $\psi(x) \sim x$.
- [[explicit-formula]]: moving the Perron contour all the way to the left expresses $\psi(x)$ as $x$ minus a sum over the zeros of $\zeta$, plus simple terms.
- [[quasi-rh]]: the 2026 claim described above lists a Mellin continuation among its ingredients.
- [[dirichlet-series]]: Perron's formula is the general bridge from analytic properties of $\sum a_n n^{-s}$ to the size of $\sum_{n\le x}a_n$.

1. Show that the Mellin transform of $e^{-x^2}$ is $\tfrac12\Gamma(s/2)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, and that the Mellin transform of $e^{-\pi n^2 x}$ is $\pi^{-s}n^{-2s}\Gamma(s)$.
2. Prove the scaling and summation rules, including the conditions for absolute convergence.
3. With $\zeta(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} + \gamma + O(s-1)$, show that the residue of $\zeta(s)^2x^s/s$ at $s = 1$ is $x\log x + (2\gamma - 1)x$. (This is the main term of $\sum_{n\le x}d(n)$ predicted by Perron's formula.)
4. Show directly from the definition that $I(y,T)$ is real for every $y > 0$ and $T > 0$.

blocks.body:
Power series $\sum a_n z^n$ are the natural generating functions for additive problems, because $z^m z^n = z^{m+n}$. For multiplicative problems one wants terms that multiply according to the index, and since $m^{-s}n^{-s} = (mn)^{-s}$, the right objects are Dirichlet series $\sum a_n n^{-s}$. Multiplying two of them corresponds to Dirichlet convolution of the coefficients, and when the coefficients are multiplicative the series splits into a product over primes.

That product, found by Euler in 1737 for $a_n = 1$, is unique factorisation written as an identity between functions. It gives a proof that $\sum 1/p$ diverges, and it is the first link between the primes and the analytic behaviour of a function.

blocks.title: Dirichlet series
blocks.body:
A Dirichlet series is a series
$$F(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{a_n}{n^s},$$
where the $a_n$ are complex numbers and $s = \sigma + it$ is a complex variable. Here $n^{-s} = e^{-s\log n}$, so $|n^{-s}| = n^{-\sigma}$. The series is the generating function of the arithmetic function $n \mapsto a_n$.

blocks.title: Where a Dirichlet series converges
blocks.body:
Since $|a_n n^{-s}| = |a_n|n^{-\sigma}$ depends only on $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$, absolute convergence is decided by the real part alone: if $\sum|a_n|n^{-\sigma_0}$ converges, so does $\sum|a_n|n^{-\sigma}$ for every $\sigma \ge \sigma_0$. Hence the series converges absolutely in a right half-plane $\sigma > \sigma_a$ (and perhaps on its boundary line), where $\sigma_a \in [-\infty, \infty]$ is the abscissa of absolute convergence. Where a power series has discs, a Dirichlet series has half-planes.

Examples. For $a_n = 1$ we get $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$ with $\sigma_a = 1$. If $|a_n| \le Cn^k$ then $\sigma_a \le k+1$. The alternating series $\sum(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s}$ also has $\sigma_a = 1$, yet for real $s > 0$ it converges by the alternating series test, and with partial summation one shows it converges for all $\sigma > 0$. So convergence and absolute convergence can hold in different half-planes. The gap is at most 1: if the series converges at $s_0$, its terms are bounded, $|a_n|n^{-\sigma_0} \le C$, so it converges absolutely for $\sigma > \sigma_0 + 1$.

On each half-plane $\sigma \ge \sigma_a + \varepsilon$ the series converges uniformly (Weierstrass M-test with $\sum|a_n|n^{-\sigma_a-\varepsilon}$), so $F$ is holomorphic for $\sigma > \sigma_a$ and can be differentiated term by term: $F'(s) = -\sum a_n(\log n)n^{-s}$. We also quote the uniqueness theorem: if two Dirichlet series converge absolutely and agree for all sufficiently large real $s$, their coefficients are equal. So $F$ determines its coefficients.

blocks.title: Products and Dirichlet convolution
blocks.body:
If $F(s) = \sum a_n n^{-s}$ and $G(s) = \sum b_n n^{-s}$ both converge absolutely at $s$, then so does the series below, and
$$F(s)\,G(s) = \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(a*b)(n)}{n^s}, \qquad (a*b)(n) = \sum_{d\mid n}a_d\,b_{n/d}.$$

The double series $\sum_{d,e\ge1}a_d b_e(de)^{-s}$ converges absolutely: the sum of the absolute values of its terms is $\bigl(\sum_d|a_d|d^{-\sigma}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_e|b_e|e^{-\sigma}\bigr)$. An absolutely convergent double series may be summed in any order. Grouping the terms by the value of $n = de$ gives $\sum_n n^{-s}\sum_{de = n}a_d b_e$, which is the claim, and also shows that $\sum_n|(a*b)(n)|n^{-\sigma}$ is finite.

blocks.title: A dictionary
blocks.body:
Combined with the convolution identities of [[mobius]] and the functions of [[arithmetic-functions]], the theorem gives a small dictionary. Write $\tau(n)$ for the number of divisors, $\sigma(n)$ for their sum (not to be confused with $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$), $\mathrm{id}(n) = n$, and note that $\sum n\cdot n^{-s} = \zeta(s-1)$.
- $\zeta(s)^2 = \sum\tau(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, since $\tau = 1 * 1$.
- $1/\zeta(s) = \sum\mu(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, since $\mu * 1 = \varepsilon$, the identity for convolution ($\varepsilon(1) = 1$ and $\varepsilon(n) = 0$ for $n > 1$).
- $\zeta(s)\zeta(s-1) = \sum\sigma(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 2$, since $\sigma = 1 * \mathrm{id}$.
- $\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s) = \sum\varphi(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 2$, since $\varphi = \mu * \mathrm{id}$.
- $-\zeta'(s) = \sum(\log n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, by term-by-term differentiation.

The second line has an immediate consequence: $\zeta(s) \ne 0$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, because $\zeta(s)\cdot\sum\mu(n)n^{-s} = 1$ there.

blocks.title: Euler product
blocks.body:
Let $a$ be multiplicative, and suppose $\sum_n|a_n|n^{-\sigma} < \infty$, where $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$. Then
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{n^s} = \prod_p\Bigl(1 + \frac{a_p}{p^s} + \frac{a_{p^2}}{p^{2s}} + \cdots\Bigr),$$
the product over all primes converging as the limit of the partial products over $p \le P$. If $a$ is completely multiplicative, each factor is a geometric series and
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{n^s} = \prod_p\frac{1}{1 - a_p p^{-s}}.$$
For $a_n = 1$ this is Euler's product $\zeta(s) = \prod_p(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$, valid for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.

Each factor converges absolutely, since its terms are among those of $\sum|a_n|n^{-\sigma}$; in the completely multiplicative case this forces $|a_p p^{-s}| < 1$, so the geometric series formula applies. Fix $P$ and multiply out the finitely many factors with $p \le P$. A typical product of terms is $a_{p_1^{k_1}}\cdots a_{p_r^{k_r}}(p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r})^{-s}$, and by multiplicativity it equals $a_n n^{-s}$ with $n = p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}$. By the [[fta|fundamental theorem of arithmetic]], every $n$ whose prime factors are all at most $P$ arises exactly once, and no other $n$ arises. (Multiplying finitely many absolutely convergent series and rearranging is legitimate.) Therefore
$$\prod_{p\le P}\Bigl(\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{a_{p^k}}{p^{ks}}\Bigr) = \sum_{n:\ p\mid n\,\Rightarrow\, p\le P}\frac{a_n}{n^s}.$$
Every $n$ missing on the right has a prime factor larger than $P$, so $n > P$, and the difference from the full series is at most $\sum_{n>P}|a_n|n^{-\sigma}$. This tail tends to $0$ as $P \to \infty$.

blocks.title: Euler's proof that the sum of 1/p diverges
blocks.body:
Take $s > 1$ real in Euler's product and take logarithms: $\log\zeta(s) = \sum_p -\log(1 - p^{-s})$. For $0 < u \le \tfrac12$ we have $-\log(1-u) = u + \tfrac{u^2}{2} + \tfrac{u^3}{3} + \cdots \le u + \tfrac{u^2}{2}(1 + u + u^2 + \cdots) \le u + u^2$. Since $p^{-s} \le \tfrac12$,
$$\log\zeta(s) \le \sum_p\frac{1}{p^s} + \sum_p\frac{1}{p^{2s}} < \sum_p\frac{1}{p^s} + 1,$$
because $\sum_p p^{-2s} < \sum_{n\ge2}n^{-2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} - 1 < 1$. On the other hand, comparing the sum with an integral, $\zeta(s) > \int_1^\infty x^{-s}\,dx = \frac{1}{s-1}$. Hence
$$\sum_p\frac{1}{p^s} > \log\frac{1}{s-1} - 1,$$
which tends to infinity as $s \to 1^+$. If $\sum_p 1/p$ converged, to $S$ say, then $\sum_p p^{-s} \le S$ for every $s > 1$, a contradiction. So $\sum_p 1/p$ diverges. This is far stronger than the infinitude of primes: the primes are dense enough that their reciprocals have an infinite sum, whereas the reciprocals of the squares have a finite one. A version with explicit inequalities is Example 3.

blocks.title: An Euler-product calculation
blocks.body: Let $\omega(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of $n$. Express $\sum_{n\ge1}2^{\omega(n)}n^{-s}$ in terms of $\zeta$, and deduce a formula for $2^{\omega(n)}$ as a convolution.
blocks.solution:
The function $2^{\omega(n)}$ is multiplicative, with value $2$ at every prime power $p^k$, $k \ge 1$. With $u = p^{-s}$ the Euler factor is
$$1 + 2u + 2u^2 + \cdots = 1 + \frac{2u}{1-u} = \frac{1+u}{1-u} = \frac{1-u^2}{(1-u)^2}.$$
Since $\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1} = \zeta(s)$ and $\prod_p(1 - p^{-2s}) = 1/\zeta(2s)$, we get, for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{2^{\omega(n)}}{n^s} = \frac{\zeta(s)^2}{\zeta(2s)}.$$
Now read the right side as a product of Dirichlet series: $\zeta(s)^2 = \sum\tau(n)n^{-s}$, and $1/\zeta(2s) = \sum_m\mu(m)m^{-2s}$ is the series of the function equal to $\mu(m)$ at $n = m^2$ and $0$ at non-squares. By the convolution theorem and uniqueness of coefficients,
$$2^{\omega(n)} = \sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)\,\tau(n/d^2).$$
Check with $n = 12$: $\omega(12) = 2$, so the left side is $4$; on the right, $d \in \{1, 2\}$ gives $\tau(12) - \tau(3) = 6 - 2 = 4$.

blocks.title: Counting squarefree numbers
blocks.body: Let $Q(x)$ be the number of squarefree integers $n \le x$. Show that $Q(x) = \dfrac{6}{\pi^2}x + O(\sqrt x)$.
blocks.solution:
The Dirichlet series of $\mu^2$ (the indicator of squarefree numbers) has Euler factors $1 + p^{-s}$, so it equals $\zeta(s)/\zeta(2s)$. As in the previous example this means $\mu^2(n) = \sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$. (Directly: write $n = a^2b$ with $b$ squarefree; then $d^2 \mid n$ exactly when $d \mid a$, and $\sum_{d\mid a}\mu(d)$ is $1$ if $a = 1$ and $0$ otherwise.)

Sum over $n \le x$ and swap the order: the number of $n \le x$ divisible by $d^2$ is $\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor$, so
$$Q(x) = \sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\mu(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d^2}\Bigr\rfloor = x\sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2} + O(\sqrt x),$$
since dropping the floor costs at most 1 for each of the at most $\sqrt x$ values of $d$. Finally $\sum_{d\ge1}\mu(d)/d^2 = 1/\zeta(2) = 6/\pi^2$ (see [[zeta]] for $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$), and the tail satisfies $\sum_{d>\sqrt x}d^{-2} \le 2/\sqrt x$ for $x \ge 1$, so replacing the partial sum by $6/\pi^2$ costs $O(\sqrt x)$ in $Q(x)$.

Numerically, $Q(10^6) = 607926$, while $\frac{6}{\pi^2}10^6 \approx 607927.1$.

blocks.title: A finite form of Euler's argument
blocks.body:
Prove that for every $x \ge 2$
$$\prod_{p\le x}\Bigl(1 - \frac1p\Bigr)^{-1} > \log x \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{p\le x}\frac1p > \log\log x - \frac12.$$
blocks.solution:
Each factor is a convergent geometric series, $(1 - 1/p)^{-1} = \sum_{k\ge0}p^{-k}$. Multiplying out the finitely many factors with $p \le x$ gives, by unique factorisation, the sum of $1/n$ over all $n$ whose prime factors are all at most $x$. Every $n \le x$ is such a number, so
$$\prod_{p\le x}\Bigl(1 - \frac1p\Bigr)^{-1} \ge \sum_{n\le x}\frac1n > \int_1^{\lfloor x\rfloor+1}\frac{dt}{t} > \log x,$$
and the first inequality is strict as well, because $n = 2^k > x$ also appears.

Take logarithms: $\sum_{p\le x}-\log(1 - 1/p) > \log\log x$. For each prime,
$$-\log\Bigl(1 - \frac1p\Bigr) = \frac1p + \sum_{k\ge2}\frac{1}{kp^k} \le \frac1p + \frac12\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{1}{p^k} = \frac1p + \frac{1}{2p(p-1)}.$$
Summing, and using $\sum_p\frac{1}{p(p-1)} < \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{1}{n(n-1)} = 1$, gives $\sum_{p\le x}1/p + \tfrac12 > \log\log x$.

The truth is $\sum_{p\le x}1/p = \log\log x + M + o(1)$ with $M \approx 0.2615$ ([[mertens]]). For $x = 10^6$ the sum is about $2.8873$, while $\log\log 10^6 \approx 2.6258$.

blocks.body:
- The Euler product needs multiplicativity and absolute convergence. For $\zeta$, the product $\prod_p(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$ converges only for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. The function $\zeta$ continues to the whole plane, but the product does not, and the zeros of $\zeta$ in the critical strip cannot be seen from it.
- A Dirichlet series can converge without converging absolutely, as $\sum(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s}$ does for $0 < \sigma \le 1$. The multiplication theorem and the Euler product as proved here use absolute convergence.
- The series and the analytic function it defines are different objects: the function may extend far beyond the half-plane of convergence. Statements such as $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$ concern the continuation, not the divergent series $\sum n$.
- Products of Dirichlet series correspond to convolution over divisors, $\sum_{de = n}$, not to the additive convolution $\sum_{i+j = n}$ of power series.

- [[zeta]]: the case $a_n = 1$, where analytic continuation, special values and zeros take over.
- [[l-functions]]: for a Dirichlet character $\chi$, which is completely multiplicative, $L(s,\chi) = \sum\chi(n)n^{-s} = \prod_p(1 - \chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$. Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions comes from these products in the same way that the divergence of $\sum 1/p$ comes from Euler's.
- [[chebyshev]]: the logarithmic derivative of Euler's product is $-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s) = \sum\Lambda(n)n^{-s}$, the bridge from $\zeta$ to prime counting.
- [[mellin]]: Perron's formula recovers $\sum_{n\le x}a_n$ from the function $\sum a_n n^{-s}$, turning analytic information into asymptotic information.
- [[dedekind-zeta]]: the analogous product over prime ideals encodes unique factorisation of ideals in a number field.

2. Show that $\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s} = (1 - 2^{1-s})\zeta(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.
3. Prove that for $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s > 1$ one has $\zeta(2\sigma)/\zeta(\sigma) \le |\zeta(s)| \le \zeta(\sigma)$.
4. Find the Euler factors of $\sum\tau(n)^2n^{-s}$ and show that this series equals $\zeta(s)^4/\zeta(2s)$.

blocks.body:
The zeta function begins as a simple series, $\sum n^{-s}$, and becomes the central object of analytic number theory. Its Euler product ties it to the primes; its continuation and special values tie it to Bernoulli numbers and to $\pi$; and the positions of its zeros control the error term in the prime number theorem.

This lesson builds the basic facts: the continuation past the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, the simple pole at $s = 1$, Euler's evaluation of $\zeta(2k)$, the values at the negative integers, and the first facts about zeros. Euler found $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ in 1735; Riemann's paper of 1859 made $\zeta$ a function of a complex variable and showed why its zeros matter.

blocks.title: The Riemann zeta function
blocks.body:
For complex $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^s} = \prod_p\frac{1}{1 - p^{-s}}.$$
The series and the product converge absolutely there ([[dirichlet-series]]), so $\zeta$ is holomorphic and nonzero in this half-plane. For other $s$, $\zeta(s)$ means the analytic continuation constructed below.

blocks.title: Crossing the line Re s = 1
blocks.body:
The series diverges at every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s \le 1$: its partial sums $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-s}$ behave like $N^{1-s}/(1-s)$ plus a constant (like $\log N$ when $s = 1$) and do not converge. To go further we need another formula for the same function. Here is the simplest. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$s\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor\,x^{-s-1}\,dx = \sum_{n\ge1}s\int_n^\infty x^{-s-1}\,dx = \sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s} = \zeta(s),$$
because $\lfloor x\rfloor = \sum_{n\le x}1$ and the swap of sum and integral is justified by absolute convergence. Now write $\lfloor x\rfloor = x - \{x\}$, with $\{x\} \in [0,1)$ the fractional part. The $x$ part gives $s\int_1^\infty x^{-s}\,dx = \frac{s}{s-1}$, so
$$\zeta(s) = \frac{s}{s-1} - s\int_1^\infty\{x\}\,x^{-s-1}\,dx.$$
The last integral converges absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, since $|\{x\}x^{-s-1}| \le x^{-\operatorname{Re}s-1}$, and it is holomorphic there. So the right side is the [[continuation|analytic continuation]] of $\zeta$ to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, and its only singularity is a simple pole at $s = 1$ with residue $1$.

Near $s = 1$, $\frac{s}{s-1} = 1 + \frac{1}{s-1}$, so
$$\zeta(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} + \gamma + O(s-1), \qquad \gamma = 1 - \int_1^\infty\frac{\{x\}}{x^2}\,dx = 0.5772\ldots,$$
which is Euler's constant (Exercise 2 identifies it with $\lim_N(\sum_{n\le N}1/n - \log N)$).

The same formula gives bounds for real $s > 1$. Since $0 \le \{x\} < 1$, the subtracted term lies strictly between $0$ and $s\int_1^\infty x^{-s-1}\,dx = 1$, so
$$\frac{1}{s-1} < \zeta(s) < \frac{s}{s-1}.$$
In particular $\zeta(s) \sim 1/(s-1)$ as $s \to 1^+$.

blocks.title: Continuation to the whole plane
blocks.body: $\zeta$ extends to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ whose only pole is a simple pole at $s = 1$ with residue $1$.

blocks.title: About the proof
blocks.body: Two proofs are standard. Repeating the integration by parts above with more terms of the Euler–Maclaurin formula ([[partial-summation]]) extends the formula to $\operatorname{Re} s > -k$ for any $k$. Riemann's own proof, through the theta function and Poisson summation, gives at the same time the functional equation relating $\zeta(s)$ and $\zeta(1-s)$, in which the [[gamma|gamma function]] appears; it is the subject of [[functional-equation]]. We use the theorem here and refer there for the proof.

blocks.title: Bernoulli numbers
blocks.body:
The even values involve the Bernoulli numbers, defined by the power series
$$\frac{t}{e^t - 1} = \sum_{n\ge0}B_n\frac{t^n}{n!} \qquad (|t| < 2\pi).$$
The first ones are $B_0 = 1$, $B_1 = -\tfrac12$, $B_2 = \tfrac16$, $B_4 = -\tfrac{1}{30}$, $B_6 = \tfrac{1}{42}$, $B_8 = -\tfrac{1}{30}$, $B_{10} = \tfrac{5}{66}$, $B_{12} = -\tfrac{691}{2730}$, and $B_n = 0$ for every odd $n \ge 3$. The last fact holds because
$$\frac{t}{e^t-1} + \frac t2 = \frac t2\cdot\frac{e^t+1}{e^t-1} = \frac t2\coth\frac t2$$
is an even function of $t$.

blocks.title: Euler's formula for ζ(2k)
blocks.body:
For every integer $k \ge 1$,
$$\zeta(2k) = \frac{(-1)^{k+1}B_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}}{2\,(2k)!}.$$
So $\zeta(2) = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$, $\zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{90}$, $\zeta(6) = \frac{\pi^6}{945}$, and every $\zeta(2k)$ is a rational multiple of $\pi^{2k}$.

We use the partial-fraction expansion of the cotangent,
$$\pi z\cot\pi z = 1 - 2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{z^2}{n^2 - z^2} \qquad (z \notin \mathbb Z).$$
It comes from Example 2 of [[fourier-poisson]], which proves $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(n^2+a^2)^{-1} = \frac{\pi}{a}\coth\pi a$ for $a > 0$. Both sides are meromorphic in $a$, so the identity persists for complex $a$, and putting $a = iz$ (with $\coth(i\pi z) = -i\cot\pi z$) gives the expansion above.

For $|z| < 1$ expand each term as a geometric series, $\frac{z^2}{n^2 - z^2} = \sum_{k\ge1}(z/n)^{2k}$, and sum over $n$ first (everything converges absolutely):
$$\pi z\cot\pi z = 1 - 2\sum_{k\ge1}\zeta(2k)\,z^{2k}.$$
On the other hand, $\cot\pi z = i\,\frac{e^{2\pi iz}+1}{e^{2\pi iz}-1}$, so with $t = 2\pi iz$,
$$\pi z\cot\pi z = \frac t2\cdot\frac{e^t+1}{e^t-1} = \frac t2\coth\frac t2 = \sum_{k\ge0}B_{2k}\frac{t^{2k}}{(2k)!} = \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kB_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}}{(2k)!}z^{2k}.$$
Comparing coefficients of $z^{2k}$ for $k \ge 1$ gives $-2\zeta(2k) = (-1)^kB_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}/(2k)!$, which is the formula.

blocks.title: Values at the negative integers
blocks.body:
Euler also found, by daring manipulations of divergent series, the values of $\zeta$ at the negative integers. In modern form they are values of the continuation:
$$\zeta(0) = -\frac12, \qquad \zeta(-n) = -\frac{B_{n+1}}{n+1}\quad (n \ge 1).$$
Thus $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$, $\zeta(-3) = \tfrac{1}{120}$, $\zeta(-5) = -\tfrac{1}{252}$, and $\zeta(-2) = \zeta(-4) = \cdots = 0$ because the odd Bernoulli numbers vanish. These are the trivial zeros. The formula with $B_{n+1}$ also covers $n = 0$ if one uses the convention $B_1 = +\tfrac12$; with the convention $B_1 = -\tfrac12$ used here, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ must be stated separately. All of these values follow from $\zeta(2k)$ and the functional equation, as shown in [[functional-equation]].

blocks.title: Zeros
blocks.body:
By the Euler product, $\zeta(s) \ne 0$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. In 1896 Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin independently proved that $\zeta(1+it) \ne 0$ for every real $t$, which is the key step in the [[pnt|prime number theorem]]. Combined with the functional equation, this shows that apart from the trivial zeros, every zero of $\zeta$ lies in the critical strip $0 < \operatorname{Re} s < 1$. These are the nontrivial zeros. Since $\zeta(\bar s) = \overline{\zeta(s)}$, they are symmetric about the real axis, and the functional equation makes them symmetric about the line $\operatorname{Re} s = \tfrac12$ as well. The first three, in the upper half-plane, are approximately
$$\tfrac12 + 14.1347i, \qquad \tfrac12 + 21.0220i, \qquad \tfrac12 + 25.0109i.$$
The [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]] asserts that every nontrivial zero has real part $\tfrac12$. Riemann's 1859 paper showed how these zeros govern the distribution of primes; the precise statement is the [[explicit-formula]].

blocks.title: The next even values
blocks.body: Compute $\zeta(4)$ and $\zeta(6)$ from Euler's formula.
blocks.solution:
For $k = 2$: $\zeta(4) = \dfrac{(-1)^3B_4(2\pi)^4}{2\cdot 4!} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{30}\cdot16\pi^4}{48} = \dfrac{16\pi^4}{1440} = \dfrac{\pi^4}{90}$.

For $k = 3$: $\zeta(6) = \dfrac{(-1)^4B_6(2\pi)^6}{2\cdot 6!} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{42}\cdot64\pi^6}{1440} = \dfrac{64\pi^6}{60480} = \dfrac{\pi^6}{945}$.

Numerically $\pi^4/90 = 1.08232\ldots$ and $\pi^6/945 = 1.01734\ldots$, in agreement with the series: the terms beyond $n = 1$ contribute only about $0.08$ and $0.017$.

blocks.title: Sums of zeta values
blocks.body:
Prove that
$$\sum_{k\ge2}\bigl(\zeta(k) - 1\bigr) = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{k\ge1}\bigl(\zeta(2k) - 1\bigr) = \frac34.$$
blocks.solution:
For $k \ge 2$, $\zeta(k) - 1 = \sum_{m\ge2}m^{-k}$. All terms are positive, so the double sum may be rearranged freely:
$$\sum_{k\ge2}\sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m^k} = \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{m^{-2}}{1 - m^{-1}} = \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m(m-1)} = \sum_{m\ge2}\Bigl(\frac{1}{m-1} - \frac1m\Bigr) = 1.$$
For the even values,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m^{2k}} = \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m^2 - 1} = \frac12\sum_{m\ge2}\Bigl(\frac{1}{m-1} - \frac{1}{m+1}\Bigr) = \frac12\Bigl(1 + \frac12\Bigr) = \frac34.$$
Subtracting, $\sum_{k\ge1}(\zeta(2k+1) - 1) = \tfrac14$: the odd values, for which no closed form is known, still have an exact sum.

blocks.title: Coprime pairs
blocks.body: Choose integers $a, b$ independently and uniformly from $\{1, \dots, N\}$. Show that the probability that $\gcd(a,b) = 1$ tends to $1/\zeta(2) = 6/\pi^2$ as $N \to \infty$.
blocks.solution:
By Möbius inversion ([[mobius]]), $\sum_{d\mid g}\mu(d)$ is $1$ if $g = 1$ and $0$ otherwise. Apply it with $g = \gcd(a,b)$; the divisors of $\gcd(a,b)$ are the common divisors of $a$ and $b$. Swapping the order of summation, the number of coprime pairs is
$$C(N) = \sum_{a,b\le N}\ \sum_{d\mid a,\ d\mid b}\mu(d) = \sum_{d\le N}\mu(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac Nd\Bigr\rfloor^2.$$
Write $\lfloor N/d\rfloor = N/d - \theta_d$ with $0 \le \theta_d < 1$; then $\lfloor N/d\rfloor^2 = N^2/d^2 + E_d$ with $|E_d| \le 2N/d$. So
$$C(N) = N^2\sum_{d\le N}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2} + O\Bigl(N\sum_{d\le N}\frac1d\Bigr) = \frac{N^2}{\zeta(2)} + O(N\log N),$$
using $\sum_d\mu(d)/d^2 = 1/\zeta(2)$ and $\sum_{d>N}d^{-2} \le 1/N$. Dividing by $N^2$, the probability is $6/\pi^2 + O(\log N/N)$. For $N = 1000$ there are $608383$ coprime pairs, a proportion of $0.6084$, against $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.6079$.

blocks.body:
- "$1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots = -\tfrac{1}{12}$" is not a statement about the series, which diverges. What is true is that the continuation of $\sum n^{-s}$ from $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ takes the value $-\tfrac{1}{12}$ at $s = -1$. A legitimate shadow of it: the smoothed sum $\sum_n n e^{-n/N}$ equals $N^2 - \tfrac{1}{12} + O(N^{-2})$, with constant term $\zeta(-1)$ (see [[functional-equation]]).
- The series and the Euler product are valid only for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. Nonvanishing "because of the Euler product" says nothing inside the critical strip.
- The formula $\zeta(-n) = -B_{n+1}/(n+1)$ is for $n \ge 1$; at $n = 0$ it depends on the sign convention for $B_1$.
- No closed form is known for $\zeta(3), \zeta(5), \dots$. Apéry proved in 1978 that $\zeta(3)$ is irrational; whether $\zeta(5)$ is irrational is unknown.
- $\zeta$ has a pole at $s = 1$ but is finite at every other point of the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, and its nonvanishing there is a theorem (1896), not a triviality.

- [[functional-equation]]: Riemann's symmetry between $s$ and $1-s$, which completes the continuation, explains the trivial zeros and produces the values $\zeta(-n)$.
- [[pnt]]: Perron's formula ([[mellin]]) applied to $-\zeta'/\zeta$, together with $\zeta(1+it) \ne 0$, gives $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$.
- [[l-functions]]: replacing $1$ by a Dirichlet character $\chi(n)$ gives $L(s,\chi)$, which detects primes in arithmetic progressions.
- [[dedekind-zeta]]: the zeta function of a number field; for $\mathbb Q(i)$ it factors as $\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_{-4})$, where $\chi_{-4}$ is the nontrivial character modulo 4.
- [[nontrivial-zeros]] and [[rh]]: counting and locating the zeros in the critical strip.

2. Show that $\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n - \log N = 1 - \int_1^N\frac{\{x\}}{x^2}\,dx$, and deduce that $\gamma = \lim_{N\to\infty}\bigl(\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n - \log N\bigr)$.

4. Prove that $\zeta(\bar s) = \overline{\zeta(s)}$ wherever $\zeta$ is defined.
